# The Rental Market {#sec-market-rental} ## Who rents ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Warrenton is the county's clearest concentration of renters](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-renter-share-1.png){#fig-renter-share fig-align='left' fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart of the renter share of occupied households in 2024 for Warrenton, Fauquier County, Bealeton, and Virginia. Warrenton is about 37% renter, well above Fauquier County and Bealeton at roughly 21% each; Virginia sits at about 33%. Renter household counts are labeled on each bar.' width=100%} ::: ::: Fauquier is overwhelmingly an ownership county: only about 21% of households rent. For context, 33% of Virginia's households are renters. Realtors, employers, and local government interviewees highlighted this, as well. Folks come to Fauquier to buy, and there is a limited rental market. Warrenton is the exception: roughly 37% of the town's 3,985 households rent, nearly double the county rate. Warrenton represents the county's principal rental submarket. Bealeton, on the other hand, tracks with the county at about 21% of its households renting. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Reliability Bealeton's renter count is small and carries Medium reliability, so it is read as a count, not a precise rate. ::: ## What renters pay ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Rents have climbed in real terms; professional asking rents sit at the top of the market](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-rent-trend-1.png){#fig-rent-trend fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of Fauquier County median gross rent from 2013 to 2024 shown nominal and inflation-adjusted, with CoStar professional asking rents overlaid quarterly from 2016 to 2026. Nominal median rent rises from about $1,140 to $1,610; the real line is roughly flat-to-up; CoStar adjusted asking rent hovers near $1,550–$1,600, at or just above the ACS median. Town points for Warrenton and Bealeton sit near the county line.' width=100%} ::: ::: The county's median gross rent, meaning all housing costs including lease rent and utilities, rose from $1,138 in 2013 to $1,613 in 2024, adding 42% in nominal, and +10% in real terms. Renters have lost ground even after inflation. In spring 2026, an interviewee shared that, "Only about 2 of 19 available rentals were priced under $1,700." CoStar professional asking rents, near $1,604 (adjusted), sit at or just above the ACS median. This is consistent with a small stock of newer market-rate apartments pricing above the broader rental pool. This report uses the ACS median gross rent as its affordability benchmark (@sec-gaps), since it covers the full rental universe, while CoStar tracks only professionally-managed apartment communities. Town rents track the county: Warrenton and Bealeton median 2024 rent (High reliability) sits roughly within $50 to $200 of the county figure. ## Where the rental stock prices ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Most rentals now price at $1,500 or more](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-rent-distribution-1.png){#fig-rent-distribution fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of the gross rent distribution for cash-rent renters in Fauquier County, Warrenton, and Bealeton across six rent bands. The $1,500–$1,999 band is the largest in the county at roughly a quarter of renters, and shares rise sharply above $1,000; bands under $1,000 are thin. Town bars with too few sample cases are omitted.' width=100%} ::: ::: The modal rent band in the county is $1,500–1,999 and represents about 25% of county cash-rent renters. Combined with the bands above it, most renters now pay $1,500 or more. Under $1,000 monthly rentals are scarce, representing only about 14% of the county's renters, underscoring how little of the stock is affordable to lower-income households. In 2025, the MLS recorded that only 28 of 203 closed leases were under $1,700, about 14%. These data identify a median county lease of $2,450 monthly, consistent with the Greater Piedmont REALTOR's March 2026 study. This leaves a somewhat larger affordable share than the single snapshot of available rentals suggested, but the story is the same: sub-$1,700 rentals are scarce, and most of the rental market prices well above that (@fig-rent-distribution, @fig-rent-trend). The MLS median runs well above the county's ACS median gross rent ($1,613) because MLS only captures leases placed through a broker, which skew toward larger single-family homes and townhouses (the bulk of this study's rental stock) rather than the smaller apartment units that lease in-house and never reach MLS. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Data note: place-level distributions Place-level distributions are noisy; only the higher-count Warrenton bands survive the reliability screen, and they mirror the county's upward concentration. ::: ## The professional apartment market ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A small, tight professional apartment market with steadily rising rents](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-costar-1.png){#fig-costar fig-align='left' fig-alt='Two-panel time-series chart of Fauquier County\'s professional multifamily market from 2016 to 2026. The top panel shows nominal asking rent rising from about $1,060 to $1,600 per unit while the inflation-adjusted line is roughly flat near $1,550–$1,600. The bottom panel shows the vacancy rate falling from about 5% to near 1% around 2019–2021, then edging back up to roughly 2–3%.' width=100%} ::: ::: The professional rental market is tiny throughout the county. Roughly 41 multifamily properties appear in the broader CoStar inventory and there are about 998 market-rate units across 14 CoStar-tracked apartment properties. Asking rent in this professional apartment market reached roughly $1,603 per unit in nominal terms (latest quarter). In constant 2025 dollars, asking rents are roughly flat, also near $1,604. Professional operators have kept pace with, not outrun, inflation in the local rental market. Fauquier has a persistently tight rental market with little slack. Vacancy for these apartments is very low, recently about 2.8%, and under ~3% for most of the past decade. ## Rental stock by structure type ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Most of Fauquier's rental stock is single-family homes, not apartments](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-rental-structure-1.png){#fig-rental-structure fig-align='left' fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart of Fauquier County\'s renter-occupied housing units by structure type. Single-family detached homes are the largest share at about 57% of rentals, followed by 20-plus-unit buildings and 5-to-19-unit buildings; single-family detached and attached together make up roughly two-thirds of the rental stock.' width=100%} ::: ::: Single-family homes are the backbone of the county's rental market, about 68% of all renter-occupied units (attached and detached). Single-family detached alone is roughly 57% of the rental market. Purpose-built apartments (5+ units) are only about 20% of rentals, the mirror image of @fig-costar's thin professional market. This could be why so much of the rental supply behaves like the for-sale market: the reliance on scattered single-family rentals means renters compete for the same limited housing stock as buyers.[^rental-structure] [^rental-structure]: Place-level structure detail is too small to size reliably, so this is shown county-wide. ## Fair Market Rents vs. actual rents ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Metro Fair Market Rents run well above what Fauquier renters actually pay](market-rental_files/figure-html/fig-fmr-1.png){#fig-fmr fig-align='left' fig-alt='Dot-and-range chart comparing rents by bedroom size in Fauquier County. For one- through four-bedroom units, the HUD metro-area Fair Market Rent sits far above the ACS actual median gross rent; the Small Area FMR range across the three town ZIP codes falls between the two but still above the local median. The gap is largest for one- and two-bedroom units.' width=100%} ::: ::: Because Fauquier is folded into the high-cost Washington, D.C. metro FMR area, the county's two bedroom (2BR) FMR at $2,246 sits far above the actual ACS median 2BR rent of $1,437. This is a gap of roughly $800. Small Area FMRs (SAFMRs) pull the benchmark towards what locals actually experience, described as a high cost and scarce rental environment. SAFMRs still land above the ACS median rent at every bedroom size, with the Warrenton and Bealeton 2BR SAFMR ranges from $1,520 to $2,340, with Bealeton (22712) at the lowest. The practical implication in the differences in FMR and ACS rents is ultimately favorable for voucher holders, with generous payment standards, something an interviewee pointed out, as well. However, this means FMRs overstate the going asking rental market and can be a poor gauge of local affordability. The ACS medians (@fig-rent-trend) are the better yardstick for rooting rents into local reality. ## Assisted inventory & preservation risk ::: {#tbl-nhpd .cell layout-align="left" tbl-cap='Federally assisted rental properties, sorted by earliest subsidy expiration'} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: Fauquier's assisted housing rental stock consists of 874 units across 13 federally supported properties. This is a small cushion against the market rents documented above. The program mix locally is dominated by Low-Income Housing Tax Credit deals, with a handful of older project-based Section 8, PRAC/811 (elderly/disabled project rental assistance), and USDA Rural Housing (515) properties whose subsidies are the closest to expiring. Rental affordability preservation at these properties is a real risk and near-term, with the soonest subsidy expiration in January 2027. Additionally, 8 of the 13 properties have a subsidy expiring by 2036, the window in which preservation decisions must be made. As assistance units are aging, the quality of these rentals throughout the county is likely lower comparatively to the other aging single family rentals. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Town spotlight — assisted units concentrate in and around Warrenton **Most of the county's assisted properties sit in Warrenton** (and nearby Remington), the same submarket that carries the county's highest renter share (@fig-renter-share). **Bealeton has little to no dedicated assisted inventory** in the NHPD record, so the affordable options there are effectively limited to whatever scattered single-family and market-rate units price low, which @fig-rent-distribution **shows is a shrinking share**. :::
